analysis_trace: Evidence synthesis: MPACT trial established gemcitabine+nab-paclitaxel (GnP) as standard first-line therapy for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with median OS ~8.5-8.7 months. Both arms receive GnP; active arm adds structured endocrinology follow-up with metformin/insulin optimization.

Mechanism: Type 3c diabetes is common in pancreatic cancer. Observational studies suggest metformin and good glycemic control associate with improved survival (evidence_role: indirect_direction). Evidence sources: https://doi.org/10.1211/pj.2013.11129176 (GnP efficacy), https://doi.org/10.3892/mco.2017.1541 (metformin meta-analysis), https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41862798 (glycemic control association).
Primary endpoint (OS): Timeframe '2 months' likely early assessment; median OS predicted ~8-9 months per GnP historical data. Active diabetes management may confer modest benefit (HR ~0.85).
Secondary-0 (PFS): Similar modest benefit predicted (HR ~0.88) given diabetes management may reduce inflammation.
Secondary-1 (Glucose): Active management expected to achieve greater fasting glucose reduction vs standard care (mean difference -30 mg/dL). High confidence given direct mechanism.
Secondary-2 (HbA1c): Active management expected to improve control rates, though 1-month assessment is early for HbA1c changes.

Uncertainty: No direct RCT evidence for intensive diabetes management in pancreatic cancer. Registry record unavailable (HTTP 403). Relies on indirect observational studies. Timeframe '2 months' for OS/PFS ambiguous.

Trial success: Uncertain. Modest OS benefit possible but may not reach statistical significance with n=210 (HR 0.85 requires ~400-500 events for 80% power). Secondary glucose endpoints likely positive.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT07272109 is a Phase 3 randomized parallel-group study comparing active anti-diabetic treatment plus chemotherapy (nab-paclitaxel + gemcitabine) versus regular anti-diabetic treatment plus same chemotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer patients with diabetes (Type 3c). Primary endpoint is OS at 2 months; secondary endpoints include PFS at 2 months, fasting blood glucose changes at 1 month, and HbA1c control rate at 1 month.

Evidence base: No direct results available for this specific trial (NOT_YET_RECRUITING, primary completion Dec 2027). Retrieved evidence includes: (1) nab-paclitaxel + gemcitabine standard of care for metastatic pancreatic cancer with median OS ~8-11 months from MPACT trial; (2) metformin and diabetes management in pancreatic cancer shows mixed results - observational studies suggest HR 0.78 for OS benefit but RCTs (including phase 2 metformin + gemcitabine/erlotinib) showed no significant survival improvement; (3) active diabetes management improves glycemic control but survival impact in pancreatic cancer remains uncertain.
Endpoint-specific analysis:

primary-0 (OS): Standard nab-paclitaxel/gemcitabine provides median OS ~8-11 months. Active diabetes management may improve metabolic control but RCT evidence for survival benefit is weak. Predicted median OS ~8.5 months for both arms with possible small benefit (HR ~0.85-0.90) for active management, but high uncertainty given lack of phase 3 data. Direction: higher_is_better.
secondary-0 (PFS): Standard regimen PFS ~5-6 months. Similar considerations as OS. Predicted median PFS ~5.5 months. Direction: higher_is_better.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC9139531 PMID: 35626020 Abstract Simple Summary Pancreatic cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The poor survival associated with this disease is due to delayed diagnosis, a lack of reliable biomarkers, and tumour resistance to treatment. Currently, surgery is the only curative treatment option, but few patients are eligible for this procedure. Developing resistance to current chemotherapies such as gemcitabine has led to a reduction in effective therapy options for patients and an urgent requirement for the development of novel therapeutic avenues. Potential success has been noted in therapeutic approaches such as synthetic lethality and immunotherapy. An array of clinical trials are currently recruiting, primarily in the area of monoclonal antibodies in combination with other therapies such as chemotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. This review article aims to highlight the potential these therapies have to improve patient prognosis and survival. Abstract Pancreatic cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related death worldwide. This is due to delayed diagnosis and resistance to traditional chemotherapy. Delayed diagnosis is often due to the broad range of non-specific symptoms that are associated with the disease. Resistance to current chemotherapies, such as gemcitabine, develops due to genetic mutations that are either intrinsic or acquired. This has resulted in poor patient prognosis and, therefore, justifies the requirement for new targeted therapies. A synthetic lethality approach, that targets specific loss-of-function mutations in cancer cells, has shown great potential in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Immunotherapies have also yielded promising results in the development of new treatment options, with several currently undergoing clinical trials. The utilisation of monoclonal antibodies, immune checkpoint inhibitors, adoptive cell transfer, and vaccines have shown success in several neoplasms such as breast cancer and B-cell malignancies and, therefore, could hold the same potential in PDAC treatment. These therapeutic strategies could have the potential to be at the forefront of pancreatic cancer therapy in the future. This review focuses on currently approved therapies for PDAC, the challenges associated with them, and future directions of therapy including synthetically lethal approaches, immunotherapy, and current clinical trials. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC5517652 PMID: 28724893 Abstract We conducted a meta-analysis to analyse the effect of metformin on survival of pancreatic cancer patients at various stages. We performed a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Web of Science to identify all relevant studies. Summary hazard ratios (HR) of survival and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated with a fixed or random effects model according to inter-study heterogeneity. Nine retrospective cohort studies and two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were eligible. There was a significant improvement in survival (HR = 0.86, 95% CI 0.76–0.97; P < 0.05) in the metformin group compared with control. Subgroup analysis indicated that metformin improved survival in patients with resection (HR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.91; P < 0.05) and patients with locally advanced tumors (HR = 0.68, 95% CI 0.55–0.84; P < 0.05) but not in patients with metastatic tumors, even when RCT data were included (HR = 0.99, 95% CI 0.70–1.40; P > 0.05), or were excluded (HR = 0.89, 95% CI 0.61–1.31; P > 0.05). This meta-analysis indicated that the effect of metformin does correlate with tumor stage but should be prudently considered given the limited and variable studies performed to data. Introduction Pancreatic cancer is among the most lethal of malignancies 1 – 4 . Each year, 53,000 new cases are diagnosed with this disease, which leads to approximately 42,000 deaths annually in the United States 5 . Limited advances have been made regarding treatment developments and the disease prognosis remains poor, with the 5-year overall survival rate ranging from 3–6% with a median survival of < six months 6 – 9 . Even in patients at early stages of the disease who receive surgical resection, the 5-year survival rate is no more than 24% due to a high rate of local recurrence and metastasis 10 – 13 . Type 2 diabetes mellitus is considered to play important roles in tumorigenesis and development of pancreatic cancer. Insulin resistance and up-regulated insulin-like growth factor I in type 2 diabetes mellitus are proposed to be the mechanisms underpinning the disease onset. Metformin is an antidiabetic drug commonly prescribed for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Recently, increasing evidence has indicated that metformin can decrease the risk of developing pancreatic cancer in patients with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus 14 , 15 . However, this effect has not been observed with other antidiabetic agents. Moreover, subsequent experimental studies have also confirmed the antitumor effect of metformin both in vitro and in vivo , which provided a rationale for clinical use of metformin in cancer treatment. However, there is still no consensus relating to the use of metformin in pancreatic cancer. Several meta-analyses have shown that metformin decreases the risk of pancreatic cancer 16 – 21 but only one meta-analysis has been conducted, which explored the association between metformin and survival of pancreatic cancer patients 22 . In the meta-analysis, four studies were included and the results showed no evidence for metformin being either harmful or beneficial with regard to survival of pancreatic cancer patients (HR = 0.80, 95% CI 0.62–1.03; P > 0.05). However, some studies have suggested that the effect of metformin delivery varied among pancreatic cancer patients with different tumor stage, and therefore analysis of subgroups by tumor stage was performed 23 – 27 . In addition, all studies involved in the meta-analysis were cohort studies, and the results of two RCTs 28 , 29 have been published recently. Consequently, further meta-analysis is required. To this end, we performed a meta-analysis on nine cohort studies 23 – 27 , 30 – 33 and two RCTs in order to determine the effect of metformin on survival of pancreatic cancer patients. In addition, subgroup analysis was performed to determine whether tumor stage affected the response to metformin. Department of Nutrition, Norwalk Hospital, Nuvance Health, Norwalk, CT, United States See more Article metrics View details Abstract Purpose: Impaired glucose metabolism is present in most patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Whereas previous studies have focused on pre-treatment glycemic indices and prognosis in those with concomitant diabetes, the effects of glycemic control during chemotherapy treatment on prognosis, in patients with and without diabetes, have not been well characterized. We examined the relationship between early glycemic control and overall survival (OS) in a cohort of patients with advanced PDAC treated in a community setting. Patients and Methods: Seventy-three patients with advanced PDAC (38% with diabetes) receiving chemotherapy while participating in a biobanking clinical trial were included. Clinical characteristics and laboratory results during 1 year were obtained from the electronic medical record. Kaplan-Meier estimate, log-rank test and hazard ratios were computed to assess the effect of glycemic control on OS. analysis_trace.finding: Phase 3 randomized trial (NCT07272109) comparing active anti-diabetic treatment plus nab-paclitaxel/gemcitabine vs regular anti-diabetic treatment plus same chemotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer patients with diabetes (Type 3c). Status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING. Expected completion: 2027-12-30.

Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma patients with diabetes mellitus (history or newly diagnosed), ECOG 0-2, age 18-80. Target enrollment: 210 patients. This is a specific subset with Type 3c diabetes related to pancreatic cancer.

Active anti-diabetic treatment (metformin, insulin, proactive monitoring) aims to improve glycemic control which may enhance chemotherapy efficacy and survival. Metformin has shown anti-tumor effects in preclinical studies but RCT evidence in metastatic pancreatic cancer is mixed.

Primary endpoint OS (2-month timeframe likely refers to assessment window). Secondary endpoints: PFS (2-month), blood glucose control (1-month), HbA1c control (1-month). Short timeframes suggest early assessment points, not median survival duration.

MPACT trial established nab-paclitaxel+gemcitabine median OS ~8.5 months in metastatic pancreatic cancer. Metformin meta-analysis shows no survival benefit in metastatic disease (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.70-1.40). Glycemic control studies show association with survival but causality unproven. Active monitoring may improve glucose control metrics.

1) Trial underpowered to detect modest OS differences; 2) Metformin RCTs negative in advanced disease; 3) Short endpoint timeframes may miss clinically meaningful survival differences; 4) Recruitment challenges for specialized population.

No direct evidence for 'active anti-diabetic treatment' vs 'regular' in this specific population. No published results from this trial. Metformin RCT evidence is indirect (different populations, protocols). Glycemic control-survival relationship is observational only.
